blocks.x:
Interview with Ed Garland
by
Bert Turetsky

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
P R O C E E D I N G S

This is April 22nd, and my name is Bert Turetsky, and I'm here with Ed 'Tootie' Garland, professionally known as Tootie, and that's what we're going to call him today. And, Mr. Garland, at this time, is, I believe, the oldest professionally active string bass player anywhere. That means America and Europe. And it's our pleasure to have him here talking to us for the jazz archives. So, Tootie, it's very nice that you could come here today. And what we thought we'd do was try to get the real story from you. How does that sound?
Okay. So what we're going to do is we're going to tell it like it was. All right?
Great. So, some of the books tell us that you were born in 1895, and let's correct that.
And you were born in New Orleans?
Okay. Could you tell us a little bit about the early -- about your early days. Were your parents in music, Tootie?
Yeah. Want me to tell you how it started out?

I first started with guitar. Then, I didn't care so much about the guitar. I jumped into it. My brother played mandolin, you know, and I finally picked up the mandolin and tried to play it, and it looked like I got to play the mandolin pretty fair. And I stayed on the mandolin for a while. Then I got crazy about bass.

My brother had a bass. He bought a bass from Sam Nicholson. And he used to tell me to never touch this bass. I'd say, 'Don't worry, Johnny. I ain't going to mess with the bass.' He said, 'You'd better not.' I said, okay, brother. So one day I looked up at that bass, you know, and I said, 'I believe I can play this bass.' I went and got the bass, and I started to messing around with it, and my grandmother said to me, 'Put that bass down. You know your brother don't want you to play that bass.' I said, 'Please let me play it a little bit. He'll never know. I ain't going to hurt it.' 'No, no. You might break the bass.' I said, 'I can't break it.' She said, 'Go ahead, but be very careful.' So I kept playing. I didn't know what I was doing, but I imagined I was playing. So finally, that evening, when he come home, I said, 'Johnny, I think I can play this bass.' 'You think you can play it?' I said, 'Yeah.' 'You been messing around with the bass?' I said, 'No, no, no. But I

just think I can play it." He said, "I'm going to see." So he went and got the guitar. He got the guitar, and the first thing, he started to make a few chords. He played a C, you know. So he says to me, "Let me see what you can do. You say you can play the bass." So I grabbed the bass, and the first thing I hit was F.
He said, "Now, what's the next chord you're going to make?" I made a B-flat, you know. Cross the fingerboard, from B-flat to F to C.
I didn't know what to do after that F and B-flat, you know.

And he said, "Now, just go right straight across there now, on that A string." And I hit the A-string, and it went, whoomp. He said, "You know what you're making?" I said, "No." He said, "That's C." So I said, "Oh, that's C, huh?" So I made C, F and B-flat. So he says, "I'll tell you what I'm going to do. I'm going to show you a few chords on this bass and I want you to practice. When I come back this evening, I want to find out how much you learned. Will you do that?" I said, "Sure. I can do it." And I done it, too. I really played an F and B-flat pretty fair. The C and G, oh, I was it there. So when he come in -- you know,
He got the guitar and he played a little waltz. He hummed it, singing it, you know, playing it. It was in C, you know.
Uh-huh. And he'd tell me 'One D, two beats'.

And I played it. And he says, 'Now, you hit this G, you hit your C, then you hit your F.' So I done that. He said, 'That's pretty good.' So that's how I started out. And I kept on, kept on, until I could play, learn the changes in B-flat and F.
A-flat. Then he taken me out on a House party, some kids job, to play for some family, you know. (Unintelligible).
He taken me out, and I laid the bass back on my shoulder, set in a chair, because I couldn't stand up to the bass, you know. I was only nine years old.

Had to play at this party. At nine o'clock. That was it, you know. I went to sleep. Couldn't keep my eyes open. I sat up there sleeping. He kept on jiggling me, you know. I said, 'I can't play no more. I'm tired.' So he got a piece of ice and started rubbing it in my eyes. The lady said, 'Don't do that to the little fellow.'

"Don't put that ice on him." Said, "Let him sit over there and rest a while. It's all right. He don't need to play." So I sat over there and got a few naps, you know, and got up again and tried to play.
Finally, I made it. And when I got home, you know how much he give me?
He paid me 25 cents. And said, "You done pretty good." "Next time I'll give you a little more."
30. Tootie, was Johnnie a professional musician?
Yeah. He was a professional. Yeah. He played the violin.
I see. Now, a lot of people wonder what the violin did in New Orleans music. Maybe you could tell us a little bit about that.
Well, the violin, you know, you take the violin -- we had a seven piece band, you know. He played all the leads, you know.
That's the lead instrument, you know.
And no piano. You had your guitar.
Your bass. Drum, clarinet, trombone, and trumpet.
And the violin played the leads.
The violin played the lead, you know. He'd always knock off the pieces, you know.
Uh-huh. Right. Did the violin player often read music, too?
Yeah. We had a group, we had a violin player name of Bigard. That's Barney's uncle.
Well, Emil would play the pieces, get his violin and play all them tunes, you know, start off and give us the cue on how to play them, you know.
Oh, you wouldn't know. Wasn't nobody could read nothing.
He played. Just that quick. Said, 'Let's go,' and he started to playing it, and the band would just play it.
Now, when the -- so, then, the violinist often read very well, and he would be the leader, sometimes, of the bands?
Right. Okay. Then, so the violinist played with the seven piece band and sometimes we're talking about the little string groups that played the parties.
Yeah. Sometimes the mandolin, guitar gets on
Would play them rags, you know, them guys play rags, you know.
Uh-huh. Did you -- like Joplin, Turpin, those kinds of things?
Oh, no. We didn't play nothing like that. No.
We played rags like the 'E' Rag, you know.
And some tune in B-flat, you didn't know what it was and neither one he didn't know what it was. You just played, you know. (Voicing of pizzicato on stringed instrument.) -- and you'd follow suit.
"What's the name of that?" "I don't know."
Sounded all right. That's how Or got Muskrat Ramble.
How did that start? Orrie wrote Muskrat Ramble, everybody says.
No. I mean, didn't you say that's how Muskrat Ramble started?
Yeah. That's the way Orrie got pretty much 'Muskrat Ramble.'
Because he had a trumpet. It was a -- no, it wasn't a trumpet. It was an old cornet. And he used to be blowing on it. On that thing, you know, trying to play it.
(Imitating sound of cornet.) -- you know? And kept on.
And we all would pitch in and add in to it -- add on to it, you know.
Keep going, adding on to it. That's (Play that again.) how it goes. Every now and then we'd add some more to it, and finally we got to play 'Muskrat Ramble'.
Well, when we got to play it pretty fair, we called it 'Muscat'.
So over at the studios, they corrected that, had that title changed. Instead of Muscat they said Muskrat.
When we went to put it on wax. Called it Muskrat.
Yeah. In fact, that whole way of composing is still alive today. Duke Ellington always did the same thing, you know. Cootie would add something in, or Rex Stewart.
Sure. And I think that's the way to go, working together.

Okay. Let's go back to New Orleans, and we have young Ed Garland there who started with the guitar and he played the mandolin, and now he's playing bass. What kind of strings did you have on the bass, Tudi, Tootie?
Gut strings. Okay. And did you use
Okay. Did Johnnie help you with bowing, or did you just pick it up yourself?
I'd go around different places like I'd go around where the Eagle Band was playing. Danny Lewis would be playing, you know.
Or Sam Nicholson, playing with the bow.
And I'd watch them. I've got a good ear, you know.
And I'm quick to catch on to anything. I'd -- so I'm just watching it, just noticing his hands, you know. Noticing every movement about him, he made on the bass.
Then when I really want to get to bowing, I went to St. Catherine's Hall, where Henry Kimball was playing.
And that was the ace bass player down
Good reading man, you know. A good reader.
And a good bower. He'd bowed a lot of times.
So I used to go there and I used to watch him all the time, you know. So he told me to put that E-string -- I used to take the E-string off my bass.
You know, to have a three string bass.
Fellows couldn't play no E-string. Didn't know nothing about making them pedal notes on there, you know.
So he says to me, 'Eddie, I'm going to tell you what I want you to do. You get that E string and you put that E-string back on the bass and play it, and I'm going to show you how to finger it.'
And which he did. (Unintelligible.) How to bow.
And the guy also showed me the bowing.
I finally done that, you understand. I used to have this slap bass business. (Imitating sound of slapping bass fiddle.) I brought that back to Chicago from New Orleans, you know, that slap bass.
Brought it clean on out to California.
But I stopped that because I was wearing out fingerboards.
I had more guts -- not guts. I'm trying to say --
Grooves in my fingerboard, you understand.
And I stopped that. I stopped playing like that. I wouldn't do it no more.
Audiences always love slap bass playing, didn't they?
The people, the folks, liked slap bass playing.
Yeah. Some of it -- (Imitating sound of slapping bass fiddle.) You know. Back with your hand.
So I said, well, you ain't doing nothing there.
Just got a handful of strings and just beating it up against the fingerboard. Ain't making no notes at all.
And I quit that. So I really got onto wanting to bow. I went to -- I don't know if I can recall this man's name. He used to play a trombone and he played bass, with Paul Whiteman. His name was --
No. He was President of 47, too.
And he used to make the wildest trombone. He was a double bass man. So I'd taken lessons from him on bowing.
So I started to take lessons from him, so he says to me once, he said, 'Listen, Ed, do you intend to just play strictly Dixie?' At that time, he'd say jazz.

You know? I said, 'Yeah.' He said, 'Well, I've got a selection of concert music.' (Unintelligible) I said, 'I ain't particular about that.' He said, 'Well, I'll tell you, (Unintelligible). You don't need to try to lowering the reed.' He said, 'I've taken notice. I gave you, in the lesson, just a minute ago, something to do, and I walked out of the room, and I was doing something, and you picked up the bass and (Unintelligible).' So he said, 'What are you taking lessons for?' He said, 'You don't want to learn how to play concert.' So I said, 'I know about -- a little about reading. I'm not much on it. I ain't an expert on it, but I know my notes.' But I says, 'I'll tell you, I likes my own basis for playing jazz music.' See?
I said, 'Let them other three men up in front. They're the men.' I said, 'I'll take care of the back. I'll make my own basis.'
He said, 'That sounds pretty good. That's up to you.' So he said, but if you ain't going on the
other side of the house, I don't see no need of your doing any more. Just go ahead and play like you want."
Sure. And you've been doing that very successfully.

Oh, yes. Right. And you're still doing it, and that's great. We've heard some of the recent stuff, though. It's fine. Basically, that's the way most of, I think, your contemporaries, or your friends learned, by listening to people who played well.
And studying them. I think the kids growing up in the last 20 years listened to records more, you know.
So they listened to different people play.
And those guys over in Germany do the same thing.
They get those records and they play it just right off the record.
Right. Yeah. Yeah. Remember Johnny Windhurst and Eddie Hubble and those guys would take Louis Armstrong's -- the Hot Five things and learn all those solos.
Was it Bob Wilber, the soprano saxophone player, that knew all the Sidney Bechet solos.
Yeah. I mean, that's a way. That's one way. I guess Barry Martin got into music by listening to these records and things.
He used to follow the bands all around and come all the way down to New Orleans.
Get on a boat, he'd get on a ship, you know, and he'd come down to New Orleans, and he'd come back and stay in New Orleans. That's where he learned all his drumming.

Right. That's the way you really do learn it. Willie Ruff. Willie Ruff is a professor, Tootie, at Yale University, and he's a bass player and he's a french horn player and he plays jazz and he plays classical music, and he's brought a big jazz program to Yale, and he says that musicians like you, artists like you, got educated in the conservatory without walls. In other words, in the real world. You heard Henry Kimball, Sr., play. And you heard Nicholson play. And after that, you developed your own style and many people have come to hear you play and see what they can learn. And we grow that way, you know. I didn't -- wasn't in this
part of the country, but I did hear Pops play and I did hear Slow Drag play, and Walter Page, and so on.
And so I listened to your recordings and other people's recordings, and I learned something. And that's a nice way to learn, you know?
Sharing all these ideas and getting together. That's a lovely way to do it. But, oh, let's get back to our story.
I tried to -- I wouldn't try to imitate nobody else. I wanted my own style.
I developed my own style. And then I had them same guys I was watching come to me.
I developed my own style and still got my own style.

I heard a demonstration earlier, and the next time we get together we're going to tape some of your own style. We're going to hear the Closer Walk on tape, which is great. So you then -- you were a professional musician at what age, Tootie? How old were you when you became a professional?
I got to be a professional in -- really,
Because all those bandleaders, they all liked me. There was something about it, I was friendly with all of them.
I'd take Manuel Perez. Dusen. Frankie Dawson.

Robichaux. They all -- they used to call me The Kid. "Let's get The Kid." All them bass players was coming over to me and stick me up on that stand, you understand, to play. And I played, and they'd shake their heads. I'm growing fast. And I was growing fast, if I have to say it myself. Done fine with the Eagle Band, I done fine with the Crescent Band -- Jack Corey's band, that is.
Done fine with the Imperial Band. And done fine with Bab Frank, the Peerless Band.
Right. Bab Frank was the piccolo player. Right?
The piccolo player. Yeah. Buddy Red.
Uh-huh. At the same time, were you
No. That was in New Orleans.
I didn't play tuba until I came out here.
I was out here, I started to playing that tuba. I got -- that was about '25. (Unintelligible)
Right after I made that record. The first record that we made, about '23, '22 or '23, something like that. And I started playing the tuba.

Okay. Because some of the books say that you started with the drums, as we were talking earlier, and then say switched to tuba and mellophone in your teens, and were playing marching gigs and then went to the bass. So let's get all that straightened out now.
No, they start from the drums. They say I played drums.
I did play drums. I played the drums. I used to be the drummer in the bands, the brass bands. We'd have brass bands, you know?
You know, carnivals, and whenever somebody would die, them boys on the corner would collect the money, you know, to pay play for the band.
And give you a band, you understand.
How old were you now, when you were playing drums in these bands?
Oh, I was 12 or 13 years old.
Okay. And you were playing the bass at nine, so you --
Then I picked up on the mellophone, which we called alto --
I used to do that in the band.
And we had Benny -- put Benny to play
it. A fellow they called Black Benny.
Oh. Was he the bass drum player?
He could play the drums, yeah, very good, too.

Black Benny. He used to run around with his car full of instruments, especially because he was playing the bass and the drums, leaving the mellophone so I started playing the mellophone in the band. And (Unintelligible) -- I come to Frisco and played at the Becolier Dance Hall. That was in 1921, that was.

When I left there, we come on down to Los Angeles, to play with Jelly Roll of a Friday and -- of a Saturday and Sunday. At Leek's Lake (Unintelligible). He used to run dances there. We played down there with them. That was King Oliver's group, I was working see?

And Joe got ready and said, 'Well, why don't we go to New York?' I said, 'Yeah? Well, I'll tell you, Joe, I'm not going to New York.' 'What? You mean to tell me you ain't going to New York? Oh, you got stature, huh? You got your long haired woman, huh, and you think you're going to own California.' I said, 'No, I don't own California, but California owns me.' I said, 'I'll tell you, Joe, I can get my shoes shined the whole year round here in California,

He said, "Yeah?" He said, "You're going to change your mind." "Oh, no," I said, "I ain't going to change my mind, Joe. I ain't going back to New York." So he kept on. Every day he'd come in and he'd say, "Well, we're leaving Monday. What do you say?" I'd say, "I give you my word, Joe. I'm not going back to New York." "I'm going to stay here." "Okay." So he left and he got Bill Johnson.

Bill Johnson to play in my place, you know. Take my place. But he gets back to New York, all right, he sends me a telegram that he wants me to come on. "Make up your mind." "No, I ain't going, Joe." So I leaves California -- Los Angeles, and go back to Oakland. Joe sent me a ticket there in Oakland to come to New York. And I told him, "Yeah, I'm coming." And I get the ticket, and I had a Studebaker. I sold my Studebaker to the man where I (And this is true from here to heaven, in the garage.) used to park the car, and the man gave me my money, paid me the money, and I goes down to 16th Street there in Oakland, to the station, for the ticket, you understand, and I heard a train coming, and I said, "I think I'll go out there and see who's coming in on this train." I look up and here comes Orrie, gets off. I said, "Is that Orrie?" Yeah,

that's Orrie. Said, "Man, I just come here for you." I said, "Come here for me?" He said, "What you doing down here?" I said, "I'm fixing to go and get this ticket. I'm going to New York." "Going to New York?" He said, "Man, Abe Ed Lyman sent for you." "We're going to wait for him." And at that time, Abe Lyman had a place on Spring, near 5th.

(Unintelligible) -- something like that. A big cafe that he had. And there was a big band playing in there, and he wanted this band, and told them to come and get me. I said, "Listen, boy, I done sold my car and the man just give me the money. I just left down there on 7th Street." He says, "Man, don't go. You're a fool if you go back there and parade around in all that snow." He said, "Man, you'll make good money here. Come on, stay. Don't go. Send the ticket back." I said, "Well, what am I going to do? I sold the car." "Well, all right. Let's go and get the car back." I said, "Well, I don't know if he's going to give me my money back." I said, "Well, all right. Let's go." I walked in there and turned the ticket back. I go down to the garage and I said, "Look. Orrie just coming for me. I'm not going away. I'm going to stay here. How about getting my car back?" He said, "Are you crazy? Oh, no. You done sold that car and I paid you." I said, "Yeah, you paid me, all right." I said, "But I changed my mind." He said, "No,
I'm sorry." Orrie said, "Oh, man, come on. We'll buy a car in Los Angeles." So I went with Orrie to Los Angeles and I stayed with him up until I went to play at the 111 Dance Hall.
Uh-huh. How long were you with Orrie on and off, Tootie?
42 years. Uh-huh. That's a long time. You must have had a lot of fun with kid.
Yeah. He was a big personality. He was a lot of --
We had lots of fun together.
I was his right hand man.

All right. We're going all the way around, which I think is a good way to do it. So, we've -- we're covering a lot of ground and we're making a lot of corrections. Did you work in the -- in New Orleans, before you leave, did you do parade work with the Eagle Band?
Yeah. And the Superior Band, too.
Right. And most of the books say that Ed Garland leaves New Orleans in 1914. Didn't we say it was -- what was it? Didn't you leave in '11? 1911.

Okay. So what I wondered about was most of the books, Toetie, say that many of the New Orleans musicians leave in 1917, when Storyville, or the District, as it was called, closed. But you leave in '11. Was there more work in Chicago for you? Or, what?
When I left there, an agent come and got me to bring a band to Chicago, to play for May Elaine.
Uh-huh. And she was a singer.
She was a white girl, you know.
In blackface. And have a bale of cotton on the stage.
And when we came out and played the opening, this bale of cotton would open up.
And she'd step out of that and start to dance.
I see. And you worked with her -- did you travel on the Orpheum Circuit then?
I see. And how long did that happen, Tootie? How long did you do that?
Didn't stay there too long. Must have been a few months.
You know, when they'd go on vacation, or the theaters have a -- the actors have a vacation.
Well, that closed and Isadora Shaw got me to play for her at Dreamland. Not Dreamland. It's the Dreamland later on.
I see. And then did you get together with Manuel Perez in a band?
-- Manuel was playing out on PAULINA, and -- with Red Nichols.
They was playing in one corner and Manuel and them was playing in the other corner. Two bands in the house, you know?
And I played out there with Manuel. He had an awful band out there. Manuel got me to play with him.
Manuel was in Chicago. Manuel was rolling -- making cigars.
And I played out there with him. And he had Manuel Perez played trumpet. Eddie Atkins playing trombone. Lorenzo To playing clarinet.
Frankie [Enger] playing piano. Cantrell playing drums.
And I was playing the bass.
And that was a bad place. That was out there among some gangsters, where we was playing there.
Yeah. Chicago was full of gangsters in those days. Was Perez a hot player or was he more of a sweet player?
He wasn't no hot player. He was a sweet player.
A sweet player. And so did --
He played a lot of trumpet but he wasn't no hot man, no.
Okay. Did -- so did Teal play some of the jazz, make it go?
Did Tea play more of the solos, the jazz, the hot playing?
Yeah. The Chicago people loved the New Orleans playing.
Yeah. I wonder what happened in Chicago before the New Orleans musicians came. What went on?
Well, they played that, you know, Chicago style. Two beats, you know.
We come back there with that four beats, you know.
Uh-huh. Let's talk about that. You said, 'The four beats, you know.' Everybody thinks that New Orleans music is two beat music, but that's not true.

Yeah. That's at the base of everything, that nice heartbeat. That's good, that four beats. So maybe in the revival music, the so-called Dixieland revival, maybe some of those people played more two beats. But Pops always played four, and he always said it was always -- you played four, and some of the books say that Walter Page, with Basie was one -- was the first person to play four beats. That's of course not true. So we're setting a lot of things straight, and that's good. Did -- in New Orleans, did they like the tuba in the bands or the string bass?
Not in New Orleans. Not until later years, you know, way late.
No New Orleans, no. No Tuba. Tudi.
How about the banjo, Tootie? We were talking about that earlier.
Yeah. We were speaking of the banjo. That banjo made too much noise. They didn't want no banjos. A fellow come along with a banjo, they'd tell him no. In
fact there wasn't none playing the banjo. It was only the white boys played the banjo.
So, then, when Johnny St. Cyr plays the banjo with the Hot Five recordings, about 1924, with Louis Armstrong, then what was that about?
Oh, well, banjos was played. They was all playing banjos after that. But Johnny St. Cyr was playing banjo-guitar.
Playing a six string guitar, with a banjo FRET in it.
So, in other words, as we said, the great guitar players didn't switch in New Orleans. Maybe some of them played later, because the white market liked the banjo.
Was that the story? Uh-huh. I've always wondered, because the six string banjo is really a banjo-guitar, as you call it.
And the banjo is a four string instrument.
now, began as a banjo player, and when he played the guitar, he played a four string guitar.
That's right. That's what Eddie Condon played.
Right. He didn't make the change. Right. So Bud Scott and those people were guitar players.
Bud Scott would pick up a banjo and he'd tune it up like a guitar.
Like the last four strings on a guitar, the bass.
I see. Okay. So that clears that up. Now, how about the drummers. How did they play? What drummers did you enjoy in New Orleans days? Who did you enjoy working with?
You don't hear much talk about him.
No. I've never heard of him. hot drummer-he was A
He was a good drummer, too. Henry Zeno. A
Henry Zeno. Yes, I know the name.
There was another good drummer. Walter
He was a good drummer. (Unintelligible). That was Robichaux's
Yes. We've heard a lot about him.
Well, I was trying to call the drummers, (Unintelligible). real drummers, you know,
He came up in the later years behind (Unintelligible). me,
And Hall, too? Tubby and Ram Hall?
Is that later, Baby Dodds. He came up.
Johnnie was working on a furniture wagon. I seen him sitting on the tailgate, playing his horn, you know, running over his clarinet. I sat there for a little while.

And I went up to him and I said, 'Say, how would you like to play in a band?' 'All right.' He said yeah and gave me his name. And I said, 'I'll tell Ory.' He said, 'Yeah, I'll go.' So I told Ory, I said, 'I heard a guy who sounds pretty good to me.' Sounded pretty good. 'All right. Call him over and I'll call a rehearsal.' So he had a rehearsal and had Johnnie come over, he came out there and got on the band,
How we come to get Baby Joe Fired Jimmy Psido David Dodds, was in San Francisco (Unintelligible).

He played violin. Also clarinet. And Joe let him go. So this boy Minor Hall, we called him Ram, said, 'Well, why are you going to fire this man? We're at the end of the Southern Pacific Line and (Unintelligible). He said, 'I've got a lot to do with it. I don't think it's right.' Then he said, 'Well, if that's the case, I'll go too.'

That was the drummer, (Unintelligible). So finally, he went to the union and told them about it -- number six -- and said, "Did you get a notice?" And he said, "No." "Did you give him a notice?" He said, "No." And they said, "Well, he done sent for another drummer trombonist." He said, "What?" He sent for Baby Davey Dodds. He's in St. Louis. Baby Davey Dodd's coming in from St. Louis and (Unintelligible). So they called in Joe and Joe -- told Joe he had to pay Jimmy -- give Jimmy two weeks, pay Jimmy for two weeks. And Ram had to get two weeks pay, but he had to give a notice. See?

MR. GARLAND: And fined Joe $200.00. Joe left for Frisco and went on back to Chicago, and he thought he was going to get by, you know. He went to open up the PLANTATION on 31st Street, near Cottage Grove. That night, everybody setting up (Unintelligible). Big band, too. 12 pieces. Joe's sitting up there getting ready to play and the business agent walked in and said, "I'm sorry. Don't nobody move." "Your band can't play here." Told the lady "This band can't play." The place is like that, you know? (Unintelligible). Joe said, "Why can't I play?" Said, "You owe $200.00 to number six. You runned off and didn't pay. So now each one of these men here has got to pay $100.00." That was $1,200.00 right there.

You see we used to use guitar in the band.
We use a violin -- so there's seven-men. That was the leader.
You use violin, guitar, bass, and drums, that was your rhythm section.
And the other three was trumpet, clarinet and trombone.
Yeah, did you like to play softer and easier with the guitar?
Oh, yes. And we would get that -- Bud Scott used to play with us.
Play that guitar. But nowadays, they -- not they put the watchacallit, the -- amplifiers --
Some of them they don't know how to tune them up and they drown out everything, just like on the bass --
They tune them things up and they so loud, you understand?
They don't know how to tune the thing up.
Tudi Pootie, do you think that jazz has got -- has jazz gotten louder through the years or --
Yes sir, it's much louder. Cause you never hear them say, comes out -- we used to call it, let's hear the feet?
Ah, Pops' spoke about that, too you know. Isn't that nice.
Right, he said, that was one of the nice things, right?
And we'd say, let's hear the feet. You could hear the feet out there, hear the people dancing.
You know, and that's why they used to use them brushes. Choo-choo-choo.
Oh, no. That's right. Yeah, I
was always interested in that because when you have a guitar without amplification, you really can't play too loud.
See, and a low register clarinet is just not a loud sound.
Oh, guitar sound so good, you know, when you play it -- when that guy strokes it right.
Do you like it when the guitar player plays four beats also, that nice --

I have got an interesting question for you, it has to do with music, but it has to do with other things. When you were younger, a few weeks ago. When you were playing your music, let's say how I can say this. Did you feel like a -- like a craftsman, like a good craftsman, when you were doing your music, or did you feel like an artist, or did you feel like both, how did you feel?
Fine, that's in -- important to know.

Do you think that a lot of the older New Orleans musicians who were -- when they weren't even full time in music, for example, when they had oh, the barbershop or making cigars, or whatever they were doing days, when they played at night did they feel like artists, too, do you think?
Well, you mean like most of the boys work in the day?
We had quite a few musicians made cigars, rolled cigars --
Take, well Barney -- well Barney's Daddy, Barney didn't do, he set up there and look at him. He didn't -- had a lot of fellows made cigars, you understand?
And work at night, play down at the Storyville District street, or New Orleans jazz, some of them be so tired they said that they sleep in the (unintelligible), you understand?
Cause they had to get up in the morning to go to roll cigars --
But they did feel like artists when they played?

Uh-huh. Because some of the sociologists have -- have not made that very clear and they felt that that happened later and I wasn't sure that that was true. I'm glad to hear that. Let me ask you, what are some of the favorite moments that you can remember now, this morning, in playing music in your lifetime, some of your -- moments that you -- could never forget?
Well one of the moments, well I'll tell you -- I don't know, all of them was all right with me. I can't say.
I got no favorite, all of them's my favorite.
That's lovely. I like that. Ah, What other music -- what other kinds of music have you enjoyed? I wrote down, for example, did you enjoy hearing Duke Ellington? Did you enjoy --
What other music do you listen to when you're on vacation and --
I enjoy listening to -- to ah, oh, those two brothers --
Dorsey, yeah. And, I also crazy about Lombardi.
I really love his playing. He's bad. And, the Brown -- Les Brown's band --
Oh, you know Les Brown's band.
I played beside Les Brown's band in Sacra -- in Stockton. Was playing for a college down there and --
It's interesting that you like Guy Lombardo. Armstrong always liked Guy Lombardo.
Many musicians just say Guy Lombardo is terrible, oh, that's cornball. --
He is indeed, he's still going.
Did they -- go ahead, go ahead.
Sweetest music this side of heaven.
You even know the commercial. Is that nice. Did -- did you hear Basie play with Walter Page. Do you know --
What others, I heard what -- what I heard on the record player this morning when I came in that was -- sounded like some happy Germans playing some New Orleans --
Yeah. I don't know what she had on that record.
Some happy Germans playing some New Orleans music this morning. How about -- jazz, oh, after 1940, did you like Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker?
Well you see some of that music -- some of that music I didn't like at all, because I didn't know what they was playing --
That's all that rock stuff, you know?
I like music, sure, but I can't get to like that rock business.
I turned down many jobs they want me to play. I say, Uh-uh. Why? I say, well there's no need for me to tell you a story, I just don't like that kind of music.
You know I wouldn't enjoy setting up there playing and don't enjoy. I like to en -- I enjoy my Playing as much as them people out there dancing or setting there listening.
I enjoy it as much as you would or anybody else that's setting there listening to me playing.
So you like music that sings and swings.

I -- that's right, I just don't like that rock business, cause I don't know what I'm playing. I play it once, done the union a favor, one night they short of a bass player and they need a bass player and the business agent come over to me, ask, working tonight, I say no. He said man I want you to work. I said, with who? He told me

somebody, forget his name, who it was. I said 'Oh, no, I don't want to work.' 'Why man,' said, 'do me a favor,' said. 'Got to have somebody that's --' I said, 'well you know I don't like that kind of music, I don't like that playing with those guys, I don't know what they're playing.' 'Oh, men go there and do something, come on do that favor for me.' I said, 'no favor.' He kept on begging. I said, 'well all right, I'm tellyou I don't get my duty!' 'Well, a good man is a good titty,' he dall them titties, you know. I said, 'well I may be good, but I -- I said all right I'll do that favor for you.' I said 'don't come back no more and ask me to play for them.'

I went down there and I forget it was Washington, and LaBrea, not LaBrea, Washington and -- wherwas that at, in -- out on Washington Avenue. I went down there they was playing, I couldn't understand them. So they played a piece said, take one, bass. I take it -- see I'm (unintelligible) you understand, they can't get ahead of me. I -- tenor saxophone player -- he's boom-boom-boom-boom.

'Give the bass one' boom-boom- 'give him another one. Take another one, bass.' Boom-boom-that's all I played, I didn't know what he was doing -- so said man that was hot, when he went out. I said, what's the name of that thing he's playing I can't think of that number. It's South Rampart Street Parade, I said, Oh, yeah. I couldn't get that thing in my mind, I know it I couldn't think of it. Ain't this awful. 'South Rampart

Street Parade," and I didn't no more know what I was playing than the man in the moon. He told me "South Rampart Street Parade, They're some -- awful breaks in that thing. Yeah. I say, yeah. Fine. Well if a man was ever glad that job was over with. It was me. Um. "South Rampart Street Parade." I know what it is.

Where -- where -- what, oh, what kind of -- I know you played for movies and you did other things, I'm trying to think of different kinds of music that you like to play. Oh, let's see, you like to play for singers and things like that?
Yeah, well that I done that for years, you know, played in night clubs, you know --
(cut) Played at the Cotton Club, Frank Sebastian.
That's right. We hit that. How about, let me ask you about a couple of other bass players, see if you enjoy their work. Did you enjoy the work of Slam Stewart, for example?
Who you played with Tatum and played with Goodman and all that.
And then Jimmy Blanton, who wasn't around long.

We just saw a picture of Arvell Arnold, he'll be out in September. He played with Armstrong. I remember Arvell Arnold Shaw from those days. We discussed some of the other bass players, last time. Oh, suppose, what would you tell a youngster who wants to be a bass player, want s to be a jazz bass player. What would you tell him to think about now?

You know a lot of these young bass players they like to take up, say for instance, me, follow me and they follow me on the stand, or follow John Doe, anybody. I always tell them, go to work and try to get something of your own.
I say, don't try to play like the other
guy. Get something of your own don't --
-- go tricking some of his stuff, you understand?
-- but try to get something of your own.
And what else should they do?
And, just pay attention to what he's doing, pay attention to the bass player, any bass player as far as I'm concerned.

If he's just starting out. You understand, and the main thing is to make sure he learns how to give them the rhythm they want. If they want four beats, make sure they learn four beats, in fact, try to play all the beats, four beats and two beats, down to one beat as far as that's concerned.
But make sure to try to get something of your own. Establish your own pattern.
Uh-huh. Should they go out and listen
to a lot of different kinds of music wouldyou say?
I used to go to the theater and I set right down and my eye'd be right down there on that bass. Watching that bass player, and listening to him you know?
Yes. So that's a good way to learn, then.

That's the way I done it. Lot of them come back and I have that right in my head, I come back, I come here, you make something on your bass I bet you that I could -- I'll go home, pick up my bass, I'll make it.
I'll bring that -- I'll bring that right on with me.
I keep that in my mind, you know, lots' of times I did. I be out in the District, going around from one dance hall to another.
Some guy make some kind of a passage, say, gee that sounds pretty good. Some time I take it and add to it.
Make something for myself out of it.
That's right. Then you made it
Right. And then that's the way to
That's the way George used to do. George used to learn things from me, cause I used to school him, you know. He used to come to my house all the time. I give him the first job he ever had.
That's what he said. That's what he said.
Yeah, he said it. That's what he said. Sure. He said that. So you would -- you would show him some changes --
Were all the New Orleans bass players friendly to each other and helpful, you seem that --
They wasn't, you know, snotty with one another.
-- play on the stand and (unintelligible) you understand?
Most bass players I know of are very nice.
You have a picture of Brow of there, Wellman Brow --
Brow's the same way, you know, I used to school Brow --
Used to have Brow come up -- with Brow come up and play, I'd get down, used to play at the Willow Lawn --

Brow'd he be up there scuffling, you know. Come on out all right.
That's nice to hear, one musician talking about liking other musicians. Bass players just do.
-- very friendly. How about other New Orleans -- did you know John Lindsay?
Herbert played the violin, Johnny played the bass.
Turned around Teddy Turner on -- start on trombone.
Yes, he was a nice bass player. I was speaking to Howard Rumsey, down in Redondo Beach. And
Howard -- Howard and I were talking about jazz bass players. And he was talking about Al Morgan.
Sure. Said Al Morgan was a very nice bass player, also.
Well all those -- all those Morgans was all right. All the Morgan -- the one who played saxophone, that's the last one died.
They all out of St. John.
La Place, John, Louisiana. The Playa St. Jordan, Mississippi.
They all out there, from there.
Morgan (unintelligible) was a nice bass player.
He liked the bow, too, like I like the bow.
Uh-huh. Did you bow sometimes when
Yeah. Like, now you say, for instance, clarinet or trumpet be playing -- he's solo, you understand? Nice and soft. I'd play kind of a melody -- melody on my bass --
I take cello, I take your part. I play cello.
Oh, honey, I played me some pretty good cello parts in it.
Sure. So in other words, it was always creative. You were always doing something different?
And when the German man asked you about routine, there that was never routine --
-- you were always being creative and making something new --
That's lovely. So that's what -- that's what keeps you young. Always doing something new and different. That's lovely. I think we have got an interview here, my friend. What'd you think of that?
Uh-huh. Well you do it very, very nicely. Do you do other solos, besides the tune that you played for us?
I like -- yeah, I got a few of them I can do.

I like it when the wind instrument, special clarinet, when he's playing something nice, You know, and you get out on that low register and play -- nice and soft. While -- I play right along with him, you understand?
I play second, I'll give him a second, you know?
